newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian businesses say time for action on reform.
newsitem.headline: Serbian businesses say time for action on reform.

text.p: Serbian businessmen on Wednesday urged the government to stop avoiding deep structural reform and said restructuring will depend on overall stability.

"Structural adjustment is a matter of life and death for Serbian economy...We always say it's high time to begin with reforms, but nothing happens," Milisav Filipovic, director of Minel machine building company, told a gathering at the Serbian Chamber of Commerce.
Filipovic said government declarations were not good enough and instead called for urgent action on reform.
"Serbia has not clearly identified targets of its long-term economic development... It remains the last country in Europe to reject privatisation," Filipovic added.
He said politicians opted for a compromise co-existence of three forms of ownership, including state, private and a vague category of "socially-owned" capital.
"We need final decisions on privatisation, which emerged as a key political issue in this country and has damaged business ties (with the West)," another businessman said.

Dragan Milosevic of the Serbian Chamber of Commerce said the survival of companies depended on their ability to restructure. He said they needed to improve management, abandon inefficient programmes and introduce new technology to attract foreign capital.
But Milosevic insisted it was impossible for any effective restructuring to take place while Serbia's political, economic and legal systems remained unstable.
He said Serbia also needed to bring its legal system in line with the West, rehablitate and restructure the banking industry, create institutional investors and develop a financial market.
Jovan Petrovic, a director of chemicals-to-publishing company Grmec called for rigorous tidying of industry.
"When we talk about restructuring we should aim at preserving only healthy parts of our economy. We must give up bad parts," Petrovic said.

The state must identify its own interest in particular economic sectors. It must determine which companies can survive on the market without any help, but also identify those with a future with a bit of the government help, Milosevic said.
Businessmen admitted radical reform will raise problems of surplus labour, potentially leading to social unrest. But whatever the cost of the reform, businessmen said it will lead to progress.

"We must aggressively push politicians to embark on reform and tell them clearly that there is no state without economy," Filipovic of Minel said. -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
